title: How do you drive a case interview instead of waiting to be told what to do?
description: In candidate-led cases you are expected to steer, and even in interviewer-led ones, proposing next steps earns credit.
hook: You drive a case by ending every answer the same way: say what the finding means for the client's goal, propose what to look at next, and ask for the data you need. Do that after your structure, after every chart and after every calculation, and the interviewer never has to tell you what to do. It works in interviewer-led cases too, as long as you accept a redirect gracefully.
body:
In this guide

  • What driving the case means
  • Propose, don't wait
  • Pick the next step that tests your best explanation
  • Summarise at the turns
  • When you get lost
  • A worked example: Coastal Brew
  • Driving an interviewer-led case
  • Common mistakes
  • Check yourself
  • Where to practise next

What driving the case means

Many candidates open well and then drift. They answer each question correctly and then stop, waiting to be told what to do. Interviewers notice, because consulting work does not come with someone telling you the next step.

Driving the case means you own the sequence of the analysis. After each piece of work you say three things: what you found, why it matters, and where you want to go next. How much freedom you get varies. McKinsey cases are commonly interviewer-led, with the interviewer choosing the next question, while BCG cases often give you more room to steer. Practices differ by office and by interviewer, so prepare to do both.

Propose, don't wait

Every answer should end with a proposal. A useful pattern has four parts:

  1. Finding: "Revenue is flat, but costs are up $9.5M."
  2. So what: "So the problem is on the cost side."
  3. Next step: "I'd like to see which cost lines grew fastest."
  4. Data request: "Do we have the cost breakdown for both years?"

Start this straight after your structure. Do not finish with "Where would you like me to start?" Instead, say which branch you would start with and why, then ask for the data that tests it. More on this moment in how to lead by proposing the next step.

Pick the next step that tests your best explanation

A next step is only as good as its reason. The strongest one tests your leading explanation directly. The weakest one is simply the next box of a framework you memorised.

Suppose a clothing retailer's online returns have doubled, and you find that return rates jumped for one newly launched size range.

Weak: "Next, I'd look at marketing."
Strong: "Next, I'd check whether the size guide changed for that range, and compare return rates by size and product within it."

The strong version names the explanation it is testing (sizing) and the data that would confirm or kill it. If it is confirmed, you know what to fix. If not, you have ruled something out and can move on. Either way the case moves forward. This is hypothesis-driven thinking in practice.

Summarise at the turns

When you finish one branch of your structure, give a two-line summary before moving on:

"So far: revenue is roughly flat, and almost all of the profit drop is delivery-app commissions. The open question is whether delivery orders make any money at all, so I'd like to look at that next."

It keeps the interviewer with you, and it keeps you oriented. It also gives you a ready-made skeleton for the final recommendation.

Every summary should link back to the goal at the top of your page: "...which matters because we need to get back to $10M." If you cannot link a finding to the goal, it probably is not important.

When you get lost

It happens to everyone. The mistake is going silent. Step back out loud instead:

"Let me take a step back. We know A and B, and we're trying to get to X, so the next thing to check is C."

Say what you know, what you are trying to reach and the gap between them. Often the next step becomes obvious as you say it. A calm step back reads as composure. Panic reads as panic.

A worked example: Coastal Brew

Here is how driving sounds across the first half of the Coastal Brew case from the casebook. Coastal Brew runs 120 coffee shops. Revenue rose from $96M to $98M in two years, but operating profit fell from $12M to $4.5M. The goal is to get back to at least $10M within two years.

After the structure

"Revenue is up $2M, so the $7.5M profit fall must come from costs rising by about $9.5M. Delivery apps launched in this period, so I'd start with the cost lines. Could I see the P&L for both years?"

After the P&L

The P&L shows delivery-app commissions rising from $1.4M to $7.4M, and ingredients and packaging from $24.0M to $26.5M.

Passive: "Commissions went up by $6M. What would you like me to look at next?"
Driving: "Commissions explain $6.0M of the $9.5M, rising from about 1.5% to 7.6% of revenue. Ingredients and packaging rose from 25% to about 27% of revenue, which also points to delivery packaging. So delivery is eating the margin. Next I'd like to compare the profit on a delivery order with an in-store order. Do we have the economics per order?"

After the order economics

An in-store order is a $6.00 ticket with $1.50 of ingredients, so $4.50 of contribution. A delivery order is $9.00, minus $2.25 of ingredients, $0.90 of packaging and $2.70 of commission, so $3.15. The interviewer adds that 60% of delivery customers would otherwise have visited the café.

"So a delivery order looks bigger, but 60% of them replace an in-store visit worth $4.50. The real gain is $3.15 − 0.6 × $4.50 = $0.45 per order. Growing delivery has mostly moved customers to a worse channel. Next I'd like to look at ways to make delivery more profitable or move customers to a cheaper channel, starting with app pricing."

At no point did the interviewer have to say what to do next. Each answer contained a finding, a so-what tied to the $10M goal and a specific request.

Driving an interviewer-led case

Coastal Brew is written as an interviewer-led case, and the lines above still work. In an interviewer-led case you may not control the sequence, but you can still interpret every exhibit, link it to the goal and offer a next question. If the interviewer then says "Actually, let's look at something else", follow them without fuss: "Sure, happy to." Driving the case is purposeful thinking, not insisting on steering when the interviewer has a set agenda.

Common mistakes

  • Asking "What next?" Replace it with a proposal and a data request.
  • Proposing the next framework box. Propose the analysis that tests your best explanation.
  • Never summarising. Without summaries, you and the interviewer both lose the thread.
  • Fighting a redirect. In an interviewer-led case, the interviewer's sequence wins. Show your thinking and follow.
  • Findings with no so-what. "Commissions are up $6M" is half an answer. Say what it means for the goal.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. You have just finished analysing costs. What should you do next?

  • Wait for the interviewer's next question
  • Summarise what you found and propose the next area to look at
  • Start your recommendation immediately
Show the answer

Summarise what you found and propose the next area to look at. A quick summary plus a proposed next step is exactly what case leadership looks like.

2. You realise you are lost mid-case. What is the best move?

  • Keep talking until something comes to you
  • Step back out loud: what we know, what we need, what to check next
  • Ask the interviewer for the answer
Show the answer

Step back out loud. Saying what you know and where you are trying to get to usually reveals the next step, and it shows composure.

3. Try it now

You have just found that delivery-app commissions explain most of Coastal Brew's profit fall. Say your next step out loud, in two sentences, in 45 seconds.

Show a strong answer

"So the profit drop is mostly delivery commissions, which now take 7.6% of revenue and explain $6M of the $7.5M fall. Next, I'd like to compare the profit on a delivery order with an in-store order, to see whether delivery adds any profit at all. Do we have the economics per order?"

Where to practise next

Driving is a habit, so practise it on full cases. Work through the course lesson on driving the case, then do Coastal Brew out loud and check that every answer ends with a proposal. With a partner, use interviewer mode and ask them to note every time you wait to be told what to do. For the exact lines at each stage, see what to say at each stage of a case.
